loci.name: registry-decay-design-lessons
loci.one_line: What specific field/workflow design choices distinguish a prompt register that avoids the CMDB/data-catalog/feature-store decay pattern from one that repeats it — not just whether registers decay in general?
loci.rationale: The contradiction graph's 'registry-survives-its-own-cost' cluster is validated: the pro-register sources (prompt-governance-is-the-new-data-governance-cio et al.) are uniformly vendor/consultancy and converge on an abstract skeleton (owner, version, approval, RBAC, retirement) with no operational detail on HOW that skeleton stays current. The counter-evidence, read directly, is far more specific and actionable than the graph summary suggests. The MLflow RFC (rfc-deprecating-model-registry-stages-issue-10336-mlflowmlflow-github) shows MLflow abandoned FIXED lifecycle stages (none/staging/production/archived) after 'extensive feedback on their inflexibility' in favor of freeform tags + reassignable aliases + one-registered-model-per-environment — a directly transferable lesson against hardcoding a prompt's lifecycle as an enum field. cmdb-vs-asset-management-differences-and-why-you-need-both makes the sharper point that dual-purpose registers rot specifically when two different owning functions edit the same record without an explicit 'who owns which column' agreement ('ITAM fields go stale... or CMDB relationships go stale... because no one has decided which one wins on which field'). why-do-data-catalogue-projects-fail adds a second, distinct decay mechanism: catalogs fail when the 'entry ticket' for the business user is too high and adoption concentrates in a technical minority, so metadata for everyone else goes stale — this is an adoption failure that produces registry decay, not a pure maintenance-discipline failure, and it is a different mechanism than the MLflow story. None of these three failure modes (rigid-stage design, unowned shared columns, high-entry-ticket curation) is addressed by the vendor sources' skeleton. A depth investigator should determine which specific design choices (auto-inferred vs. manually-entered owner; staleness/last-used signals as first-class fields; usage-triggered rather than calendar-triggered retirement; tags+aliases instead of enum stages; explicit column-ownership contracts between the register and consuming teams) are load-bearing for avoiding each failure mode, since the product's schema (Section 2 of the report) must make these choices explicitly rather than inherit the vendor skeleton uncritically.

opposing_positions.position: A centralized register with owner/version/approval/RBAC/retirement fields is the correct converged-on pattern and is sufficient design guidance.

That skeleton alone predictably decays through three separable, named mechanisms — rigid lifecycle enums (MLflow), unowned shared fields (CMDB), and high-entry-ticket curation that concentrates use in a technical minority (data catalogs) — each requiring a distinct, specific design countermeasure, not a generic 'have RBAC and an owner field.'

suggested_searches: MLflow model version aliases vs stages migration lessons learned
internal developer platform metadata staleness prevention design pattern
prompt registry owner field auto-inferred vs manual git blame
data catalog usage-based curation trigger design pattern

loci.name: build-vs-layer-defensibility
loci.one_line: Given that Bedrock and Vertex already ship free, versioned, labeled prompt-management primitives inside their own platforms, is building a standalone internal register defensible, or does the defensible design collapse to a thin sync/aggregation layer over those native tools rather than a competing store?
loci.rationale: The contradiction graph's 'build-vs-buy-commoditization' cluster names this fight but its evidence_quality_delta calls side B (vendor mechanism docs) 'establishing the scope boundary rather than an argument' — i.e. under-argued. Reading build-vs-buy-a-guide-for-internal-tools-retool-blog directly sharpens the case against a full internal build: its own diagnostic questions ('is this tied to revenue generation or competitive advantage?', 'do you have the internal resources to build AND maintain?', the 7Cs framework's 'Complexity: do existing solutions fit your needs or are your requirements bespoke?') point toward a MIDDLE answer the graph doesn't capture — build the multi-provider consolidation and governance layer (which no single-cloud vendor can offer by definition, since Bedrock and Vertex are each scoped to their own project/account) while deliberately NOT rebuilding what Bedrock/Vertex mechanism already does well (storage, versioning, label assignment). This reframes the fight from 'build vs buy' to 'what is the minimum surface that must be built because it is structurally unavailable from any single vendor' — a materially different, more specific, and more defensible design conclusion than either side of the pre-identified cluster states outright. This is load-bearing: it determines the entire architecture diagram in Section 9 of the report (thin governance/ledger layer with adapters vs. a store that replaces vendor prompt stores).

opposing_positions.position: Homegrown internal tools carry multi-year maintenance costs several times the initial build, senior engineers avoid inheriting them, and most face re-architecture pressure within 5-7 years — so the built surface should be minimized, per Retool's own decision framework (core-competency test, 7Cs).

Bedrock and Vertex prompt management are each scoped to a single vendor's project/account, so a multi-product, multi-provider conglomerate structurally has no single vendor product that gives it one ledger — a governance/aggregation layer has no 'buy' substitute at the scope the query requires, regardless of build-cost concerns.

suggested_searches: cross-cloud governance layer vs single-vendor lock-in enterprise LLMOps
Azure AI Foundry prompt management multi-provider scope
internal platform team build minimal surface adapter pattern case study
engineering blog abandoned internal prompt registry postmortem

loci.name: content-versioning-approval-workflow-gap
loci.one_line: Do existing label/content-based prompt versioning systems (Langfuse, PromptLayer, Agenta) actually implement a structured HITL approval-decision object (approver identity, evidence, timestamp, audit trail, pending/rejected states), or only coarse role-gated label reassignment — meaning the mandatory-approval-gate constraint requires building an approval state machine that no vendor's label mechanism provides regardless of the prompt-as-code-vs-content choice?
loci.rationale: Reading version-control-langfuse directly shows Langfuse's closest analog to an approval gate is 'Protected prompt labels' — an Enterprise/Teams-add-on feature where only admin/owner roles can reassign a protected label like 'production.' This is role-gated WRITE access to a label, not an approval workflow: there is no visible pending-review state, no record of who reviewed what evidence, no rejection path, and no binding link to an eval/cost delta at the moment of promotion. PromptLayer's release-labels mechanism (release-labels-promptlayer, per the contradiction graph) appears to work the same way. Agenta's non-engineer workflow (prompt-management-for-non-engineers...) instead relies on an informal 'team reviews together' step outside the tool. This means the prompt-as-code-vs-content fork in the contradiction graph is not actually decisive for satisfying the HITL constraint — NEITHER architecture ships a real approval object today. The product's promote-gate 'evidence card' (consequence diff, eval delta, cost delta, blast radius, recommendation) is therefore original scope that must be built regardless of which versioning substrate (git or label-store) is chosen, and depth investigation should establish whether any tool in the wider landscape (Bedrock, Vertex, Braintrust) does better, or whether this really is greenfield.
suggested_searches: PromptLayer release label approval workflow mechanics
Braintrust prompt promotion review gate feature
Bedrock prompt management version approval workflow
approval state machine design pattern draft pending approved rejected audit trail

loci.name: improvement-agent-differentiation-risk
loci.one_line: Given that automatic prompt-improvement agents are already shipping in a funded competitor (Braintrust Loop) and peer-reviewed evidence shows generic optimization can overfit or actively harm a specific application, should the agent layer be reframed away from 'suggests improvements' toward a capability that is not already commoditized and does not carry the overfitting risk?
loci.rationale: The contradiction graph's 'auto-improvement-agent-value' cluster already flags this as high relevance and notes side A's second source (loop-agent-braintrust) 'shows the capability already shipping in a competing product, so even if it works it is not a differentiator' — but the graph stops at flagging the tension without resolving what the agent SHOULD do instead. The query's own positioning doc explicitly anti-positions against 'an AI agent that suggests prompt improvements (already commoditized by Braintrust Loop, PromptLayer, Bedrock)', which makes this locus directly load-bearing for whether the built agent matches the product's own stated strategy. The academic side (251213598-textual-gradients-are-a-flawed-metaphor-for-automatic-prompt-optimizat, 260122025-when-generic-prompt-improvements-hurt) gives a second, independent reason beyond commoditization to avoid a 'propose-and-apply' agent as the flagship capability: training/test accuracy gaps of 5-20% and demonstrated harm from generic improvements mean an agent that auto-proposes changes without grounding in the specific org's production traffic is both undifferentiated AND risky. Depth investigation should determine what the agent's actual defensible job is — e.g., an ingestion/dedup/clustering agent (matches USP pillar 1, 'start from the existing chaos'), or an evidence-card synthesis agent for the approver (matches USP pillar 3) — rather than an optimization agent, and should check whether Loop and equivalent competitor agents scope their optimization to production-traffic-bootstrapped evals (which would blunt the overfitting critique) or to static benchmarks (which would not).

opposing_positions.position: Automatic prompt optimization measurably beats human-written prompts on benchmarks and is now productized and accessible to non-technical users, so it is a viable, user-facing capability.

The optimization metaphor is flawed, generic improvements measurably overfit and can harm a specific deployed application relative to evaluation-driven, context-specific iteration, and the capability is already shipped by a funded competitor — so it is neither safe nor differentiating as a flagship feature.

suggested_searches: Braintrust Loop agent evaluation methodology production traffic grounded
prompt optimization agent overfitting production traffic vs benchmark
AI agent for prompt ingestion deduplication clustering enterprise
PromptLayer bedrock automatic prompt suggestion feature scope

loci.name: github-duplication-evidence-transferability
loci.one_line: Do the actual quantified findings of the one disinterested empirical study on prompt scatter/duplication (24,800 prompts, 92 GitHub repos) support the product's founding premise for a SINGLE conglomerate's internal estate, or do they measure a different phenomenon (cross-project public-repo duplication) that only superficially resembles intra-org prompt sprawl across code/Sheets/Notion?
loci.rationale: coverage-gaps.md is explicit that this is 'the only evidence in the corpus that the scattered/duplicated starting state is real and measurable rather than asserted' and that it is 'load-bearing out of proportion to its size.' However, the corpus note (250912421-understanding-prompt-management-in-github-repositories-a-call-for-best) currently contains only the arXiv abstract page, not the paper's actual findings, methodology, or quantified duplication rate. The abstract confirms 'substantial internal and external prompt duplication' and 'considerable inconsistencies in prompt formatting' across 92 public repositories, which is suggestive but scoped differently from the query's premise: the product targets ONE corporate group's prompts scattered across code/Sheets/Notion/Drive/chat (an internal-coordination-failure story), while this paper measures duplication ACROSS 92 unrelated open-source repositories (which could equally be explained by copy-paste reuse of popular prompt patterns across different codebases — a normal, benign form of convergence, not a governance failure). Depth investigation must read the full paper (methodology, is 'internal duplication' defined as within-repo or within-org, what fraction of duplication is flagged as problematic vs. benign reuse, what 'quality attributes' were measured) to determine whether this evidence actually transfers to the query's premise or whether the report should flag the premise as still asserted-but-unmeasured for the internal-org case specifically.
suggested_searches: Understanding Prompt Management in GitHub Repositories Hao Li findings duplication rate
promptware prompt quality empirical study internal vs external duplication
prompt sprawl measurement enterprise internal repositories study

loci.name: spreadsheet-displacement-adoption-mechanics
loci.one_line: Given that the product's explicit win condition is 'used more than Google Sheet' by a self-described non-technical, 'lazy' primary user, what specific day-one design mechanisms (not governance features) actually cause teams to abandon a 'good enough' spreadsheet/Notion incumbent, versus what mechanisms the corpus shows fail to achieve this?
loci.rationale: why-your-team-keeps-reverting-to-spreadsheets, read directly, gives a specific and actionable diagnostic largely absent from the governance-focused sources: teams revert to spreadsheets not from lack of training but because 'the official system adds more steps than it removes,' because 'ownership of fields, stages, or handoffs is unclear,' and because reporting/dashboards inside the new system don't answer the questions people actually export spreadsheets to answer. why-do-data-catalogue-projects-fail independently converges on the same mechanism from an adjacent category: catalogs fail specifically among BUSINESS (non-technical) users because 'the entry ticket remains too high' and the tool 'becomes reserved for data teams,' while the departments 'continue to operate outside the system' — precisely the persona split (Minh/Toàn non-technical primary users vs. Quân the developer) the product is designed around. Neither source is prompt-specific, but both are disinterested-enough operational diagnostics (not vendor pitches for THIS product category) about why registers/systems-of-record fail to displace ad hoc tools, and they converge on causes (friction beats governance value, unclear field ownership, exports as an unaddressed warning sign) that are directly testable design requirements for the ingestion/onboarding flow (USP pillar 1) and the day-one UX, distinct from the longer-horizon decay question in the registry-decay locus above. This is load-bearing for Section 10 (Adoption) and Section 11 (build sequence / demo proof points) — it says the demo must prove the entry-ticket is low and the first-session value is legible to a non-technical user, not merely that the schema and governance model are correct.
suggested_searches: internal tool adoption spreadsheet displacement case study enterprise
why employees keep using spreadsheets instead of official system
low-friction onboarding internal platform non-technical users design
shadow IT spreadsheet sprawl root cause governance tool
